pages.html:
Module 3 (Q3 · Jane Eyre, "The Sovereign Self") — Teacher Standards Map

Teacher-only. Never place these codes on student-facing pages. B.E.S.T. ELA Grade 11 + Texas TEKS §110.38 dual compliance. Per-week benchmark detail and every quotation's verification list live in each M3_W*_teacher.md; this file is the module-level crosswalk and the Texas landings. Built 2026-09-21 from _S2-BUILD-SPEC.md.

Quarter 3 target B.E.S.T. benchmarks (course map) and where each lands

  • ELA.11.R.1.1 key elements and layers of meaning in a literary text: every literature lesson, Weeks 1–7 (the two narrating selves, the Gothic interior, dialogue and control of terms, the two proposals, the ending).
  • ELA.11.R.1.2 universal themes across time and place: the arc-of-the-sovereign-self lesson synthesis (Jane beside Hamlet, Publius, Emerson, Douglass); the module question itself; the outro reflection.
  • ELA.11.R.1.3 character perspective and juxtaposition: Jane/Helen (Wk2), Jane/Blanche (Wk4), the two proposals (Wk6), the experiencing/narrating self (Wk1).
  • ELA.11.R.1.4 poetry of its period: The Victorian-poem lesson Reading a Victorian Poem (Wk4) on the recitation menu poems; the graded recitation (Wk6).
  • ELA.11.R.2.1 structures and features of informational texts: The periodical-feature lesson Reading a Periodical Feature and The text-features lesson text features (Wk8), taught on a real public-domain periodical text ("Hints on the Modern Governess System," Fraser's Magazine, Nov. 1844, Internet Archive; excerpts verified against the scan 2026-09-21).
  • ELA.11.R.3.1 figurative language and allegory: the fire and wine images (Wk1), the red-room and the third story as Gothic figures (Wks 1, 3, 5), the split chestnut (Wk5).
  • ELA.11.R.3.3 contemporaneous authors and period: Situate the Text (the Gateshead lesson); the Victorian poets on the menu (Wk4); Fraser's (Wk8).
  • ELA.11.C.1.4 expository/informative writing: The Thornfield Chronicle (Draft Wk8, Final Wk9, Tier 3), scaffolded by Feeder 5 (Wk2), Feeder 6 (Wk4), the project lesson The Workshop (Wk7), Feeder 9 (Wk7).
  • ELA.11.C.1.5 revision: the revision lesson revision workshop, Draft → Final, Feeder 6's revise-a-flat-sentence step.
  • ELA.11.C.2.1 oral presentation: Graded Recitation (Wk6, 20 pts) and Feeder 9 Audio Minute (Wk7).
  • ELA.11.C.3.1 conventions and sentence craft: every L04 (periodic/cumulative/short; semicolon and colon; participial and absolute phrases; dialogue punctuation; appositives; comparison and parallel structure; MLA and quotation integration; text-feature conventions; editing checklist).
  • ELA.11.C.4.1 research: JStor Refresher (Wk3), the governess-question lesson source-to-sentence (Wk8), the Chronicle's two-source requirement incl. one JStor source.
  • ELA.11.C.5.1 / C.5.2 digital presentation and publishing: The Chronicle Online (Wk9, Claude Code builds the page from the unchanged Final text) and the publishing lesson publishing lesson.
  • ELA.11.V.1.1 / V.1.2 / V.1.3 vocabulary, etymology, connotation: every L04 Word Study (4 columns incl. "Word origin"); two borrowed foreign phrases (Wk3 tête-à-tête, Wk7 faux air with jeune encore).

Word Study words this module (none repeat M1/M2)

Wk1 opprobrium, sanguine · Wk2 veneration, mortify · Wk3 cachinnation, tête-à-tête · Wk4 sardonic, presentiment · Wk5 avaricious, profligate · Wk6 inexorable, despotism · Wk7 conflagration, faux air (jeune encore as a supporting example) · Wk8 appanage, superannuated (from the Fraser's text) · Wk9 review table, no new words.

Texas TEKS §110.38 landings in Module 3

  • (11)(A)–(D) inquiry: the JStor Refresher (Wk3) now requires a written research question, a first plan (two places to look, what kind of source would settle it), and a revised question plus one line on what in the process did not work after the first search; the project lesson The Workshop (Wk7) starts from those lines.
  • (10)(E)/(10)(F) literary and rhetorical analysis as composed genres: carried as short analytic responses with quoted evidence (weekly discussions, e.g. Wk3 setting and detail). No stand-alone analysis essay exists in the year; strong partial.
  • (3) self-sustained independent reading: Independent Reading page (M0) + Quarterly Reading Check (Wk8). Jane Eyre is the Q3 study text and is off-limits as the independent choice.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write one paragraph that explains one part of Jane's world to a stranger who has never opened the book: clear, interesting, and accurate. It is the smallest unit of a periodical feature.
🎯 CHOOSE ONE FEATURE OF JANE'S WORLD

2
Open with a lead sentence that hooks. A stranger has no reason yet to keep reading; give them one, a fact, a detail, or a question, before you explain anything. Do not open by announcing the assignment or the novel's title as if filing a report.
3
Give one idea per sentence or tight group of sentences, building the reader's understanding in order. The first time you use a term your reader would not already know, define it in your own words, right there in the sentence, without stopping to sound like a glossary.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Study how one master sentence is built, then build one of your own from the same blueprint. Imitation of this kind is not copying; it is taking a structure apart to see what makes it work.
🎯 PICK ONE SENTENCE (or choose your own from ch. 16–21)
• The inverted opener: “Amidst this sordid scene, sat a man with his clenched hands resting on his knees, and his eyes bent on the ground.” (ch. 18)
• The piling repetition: “I must watch this ghastly countenance—these blue, still lips forbidden to unclose—these eyes now shut, now opening, now wandering through the room, now fixing on me, and ever glazed with the dulness of horror.” (ch. 20)
• The compound with a participial turn: “The old crone ‘nichered’ a laugh under her bonnet and bandage; she then drew out a short black pipe, and lighting it began to smoke.” (ch. 19)
Any other sentence from chapters 16 through 21 that has a structure worth studying is fair game; just quote it exactly and cite the chapter.

2

3

Independent Reading · Quarterly Reading Check
Three Minutes on the Book You Chose
Assignment · 20 pts · one recording, one of four shapes
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
At the start of the quarter you chose a book from the Optima Independent Reading library (the Independent Reading page in Module 0 of this course explains how). This is the one check on that reading: a recording of about three minutes, in whichever of the four shapes below fits you and the book. There is no quiz, no log, and no book report. Jane Eyre is this quarter's study text and is not eligible; any other book from the library, or one your teacher approved, is.
Pick one of four
1
Oral Book Response
ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.
1
What is the book, and how far did you get?
2
Pick one character. What do they want, and what is in the way?
3
Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?
4
Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.
5
Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
2
Dramatic Reading
ABOUT 3 MINUTES
1
Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
2
Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
3
Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
3
Make the Case
ABOUT 3 MINUTES
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
1
Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
2
Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
3
Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
4
Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
5
Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4
A Different Ending
ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
1
Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
2
Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
3
Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
4
Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.
What earns full credit
›You clearly read the book.
›You point at something specific, a moment or a line, rather than the story in general.
›You say something that is yours: a judgement, a disagreement, a question.
›You can be heard clearly the whole way through.
What a summary cannot do for you
All four options are built so that a plot summary will not get you through them. Here is what your teacher is actually listening for.
›Name where you are. Give a page, a chapter, or “about two thirds through.” Summaries do not carry page numbers. Readers do.
›Read or quote something exact. One short line, said out loud. It is the fastest way there is to show you held the book.
›Say what you thought was wrong. Or dull, or surprising. A summary has no opinions. You do, and that is the part being assessed.
›Stay on one moment. Retelling the whole plot is the clearest sign of a book someone did not read. One scene closely beats the whole story vaguely.

ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.

3

ABOUT 3 MINUTES
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
1
Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
2
Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
3
Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
4

5

4
A Different Ending
ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
1

2

3

discussions.title: Is Jane's Defiance a Virtue or a Fault?
discussions.html:
At Gateshead, Jane fights back three times: she strikes John Reed after he throws the book (ch. 1), she resists "all the way" to the red-room (ch. 2), and she tells Mrs. Reed to her face, "I am not deceitful" (ch. 4). The adults call her passionate, wicked, and a liar. The narrator, looking back, calls the last of these her "first victory" and then says vengeance tasted "as if I had been poisoned."

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: in these four chapters, is Jane's defiance a virtue, a fault, or a virtue with a cost? In four to six sentences, defend your reading with one quotation from the text, cited by chapter. Say plainly what the defiance gains her and what it costs her, using the narrator's own words where you can.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Argue from the words on the page, not from how you would feel in her place. The narrator gives you her own judgment in chapter 4; use it or argue with it.
  • A virtue with a cost is a real position, not a dodge, as long as you name the cost specifically.
  • Open with a short blow (your claim in under ten words), then a periodic sentence that holds your reason to the end (the periodic-sentence lesson).

discussions.title: Helen Endures; Jane Resists. Whose Response Is the More Admirable?
discussions.html:
At Lowood, Jane and Helen Burns answer injustice in opposite ways. Jane tells Helen plainly, "when we are struck at without a reason, we should strike back again very hard" (ch. 6). Helen answers her, "It is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury," and points Jane toward the New Testament instead (ch. 6). Chapter 8 tests both creeds: Helen wears an unjust label, "Slattern," all day without protest, and it is Jane who tears it off and burns it that evening.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: whose response to injustice, Helen's or Jane's, is the more admirable in these chapters? In four to six sentences, defend your reading with one quotation from each girl's own words, cited by chapter. Say plainly what each creed costs the girl who holds it.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Argue from the words on the page. Both girls give reasons for their creed in chapter 6; use those reasons, not a guess at how you would feel in either girl's place.
  • "Both are admirable, in different ways" is a real position, as long as you name what each one costs.
  • Use a colon at least once to open your claim onto its reason, and a semicolon at least once to join two related statements (the semicolon-and-colon lesson).

discussions.title: How Does Brontë Build Unease Through Setting and Detail?
discussions.html:
Since Jane arrives at Thornfield, Brontë layers in small, unresolved details: a corridor with "two rows of small black doors all shut" (ch. 11), a laugh that recurs without explanation (ch. 11, 12, 15), a housekeeper who offers a name, "perhaps Grace Poole," and nothing more (ch. 11), and finally a real fire in Rochester's bed (ch. 15). None of these is explained by the end of chapter 15.

Post (by mid-week): Choose ONE specific detail of setting or description from chapters 11 through 15 that builds unease for you as a reader. Quote it directly, cited by chapter. In four to six sentences, explain what makes that particular detail unsettling: is it what it withholds, what it repeats, or how it is placed in the scene? A required quoted detail is not optional; a post without one will not earn full credit.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who chose a different detail than yours. Say whether their detail builds unease the same way yours does, or differently, and point to the text to support your answer.

Guidance

  • Pick ONE detail and go deep, rather than listing several briefly. A precise reading of one line beats a summary of the whole atmosphere.
  • Stay with what chapters 11 through 15 actually say. Do not guess at, or refer to, anything beyond chapter 15.
  • Try opening your post with a participial phrase (the descriptive-modifiers lesson): layered description is a tool you can use, not just analyze.

discussions.title: Is Theirs a Meeting of Equals? What Does Jane Refuse to Surrender?
discussions.html:
This week, Jane trades wit for wit with a disguised Rochester in the library, nurses a wounded stranger in the middle of the night without asking the questions she clearly wants to ask, and forgives a dying woman who once wronged her badly. In none of these scenes does rank disappear: Jane is still a governess, still poor, still dependent. And yet in each one she holds something back from surrender, whether that is her composure, her honesty, or her own judgment of what she owes another person.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: in chapters 16 through 21, is the relationship between Jane and Rochester a meeting of equals, or does rank still decide who has the power in the room? In four to six sentences, defend your reading with one quotation from a specific exchange, cited by chapter. Say plainly what Jane refuses to surrender, no matter which way the power tips.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Ground your claim in a real exchange, not a general impression of the two characters. The fortune-teller scene, the sickroom, and the deathbed all give you dialogue to cite directly.
  • "A meeting of equals in wit, but not in rank" is a real position, as long as you show both halves with evidence.
  • Punctuate any dialogue you quote correctly, using what you learned in the dialogue-and-wit lesson.

discussions.title: Why Does Jane Refuse to Remain with Rochester?
discussions.html:
In chapter 27, Rochester offers Jane every argument he has: his suffering, his years of loneliness, the unfairness of a law that binds him to a marriage that was never a real union in any way that matters to him. Jane's own feelings argue his case for him, loudly, from inside her own mind. And still she leaves before dawn, on foot, with twenty shillings, saying to herself, "I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself."

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: does Jane make the right choice in refusing to stay with Rochester, or does her principle cost more than it is worth? In four to six sentences, defend or challenge her choice with one quotation from chapter 27, cited by chapter. Name specifically what she gains and what she loses by leaving.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Argue from what the text actually shows Jane paying and gaining, not from a general opinion about the situation. Chapter 27 gives you both sides of the argument in her own words; use them.
  • Defending her choice and questioning whether it was worth the cost are not opposite positions. You can agree she was right and still name what it cost her.
  • If you introduce Jane or Rochester by name in your post, define who they are at this exact point in the novel with an appositive (the appositives lesson), not a summary sentence.

discussions.title: Duty Without Love, Love Without Law: Why Reject Both?
discussions.html:
In chapter 23, Rochester asks Jane to stay with him without a lawful marriage; she answers, "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you." In chapter 34, St. John asks Jane to marry him lawfully, with no love in it at all, telling her she is "formed for labour, not for love." She answers, "I scorn your idea of love." Two proposals, opposite in almost every way, and Jane refuses them both.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: why does Jane reject both offers, when refusing either one alone would have been the easier, more explicable choice? In four to six sentences, defend your reading with one quotation from chapter 23, 27, or 34, cited by chapter. Say plainly what each refusal costs her.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who focused on a different chapter or a different cost than you did. Point to one line in the text that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Argue from the words on the page. Jane gives you her own reasons in both scenes; use them or argue with them.
  • Do not treat the two refusals as the same refusal twice. Rochester and St. John ask for opposite things; explain what is actually being turned down each time.
  • Open with a short blow (your claim in under ten words), then use a comparison or parallel structure sentence from the comparison-and-parallel-structure lesson to hold both refusals in view at once.

discussions.title: The Thornfield Chronicle: Pitch Your Feature
discussions.html:
You are about to join the staff of a literary-cultural periodical and write an informative feature explaining one part of Jane's world to a general reader. Before you draft, pitch your angle here the way you would pitch it to an editor deciding whether to run it.

Post (by the end of Week 6), your pitch, in 4 to 6 sentences:

  1. Which angle are you writing: (a) the real position of a Victorian governess, (b) the Gothic mode and why Bronte uses it, (c) inheritance, marriage law, and money in the novel, or (d) the shape of a coming-of-age story and how Jane Eyre fits and bends it?
  2. What is the lead sentence you plan to open with, the one that has to hook a stranger in the first line?
  3. Who is your "general reader," specifically? (Not "everyone." A magazine subscriber who has never read the novel, a student researching Victorian England, a modern reader curious about the period: pick one and say so.)
  4. What does that reader most need explained before the rest of your feature makes sense?
  5. Name one source you expect to use (a text, a database, or a specific search you plan to run in JStor).

Reply (by the start of Week 7) to at least TWO classmates. This discussion requires two replies, not one, since the Chronicle depends on more feedback than a single lesson discussion does. For each reply, name one specific thing that makes the angle clear to a stranger who has never read the novel, and ask one honest question, a place the lead might confuse a new reader, a fact that seems to need a source, or an angle that might be broader than 900 to 1,200 words can hold.

Guidance

  • A strong lead hooks a stranger, not a classmate who already knows the novel. If your lead only makes sense to someone who has read Jane Eyre, it is not ready yet.
  • "Good angle" is not feedback. "Your lead assumes the reader already knows what a governess's salary tells you about her social rank. One sentence naming that rank before you compare it would fix it" is.
  • You are not co-writing anyone's feature. Every Thornfield Chronicle submission stays a solo piece; this discussion only trades feedback before the project lesson.
  • This is one discussion spanning two weeks: it opens at the end of Week 6 and stays open through the start of Week 7, so check back for replies even after you post.

discussions.title: Is the Ending a Triumph of Conscience or a Quiet Compromise?
discussions.html:
The novel's central fact arrives in four plain words: "Reader, I married him" (ch. 38). Jane tells us she has been "supremely blest" for ten years and that she has been Rochester's "vision" and his "right hand" while he was blind. She also tells us that St. John Rivers "never will marry," that he went to India alone, and that the novel's very last paragraph is given to his own words about his approaching death, not to her own household's happiness.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: is this ending a triumph of Jane's conscience, the payoff for everything she refused to give up across the novel, or a quiet compromise, a settling that costs her something the novel does not fully admit? In four to six sentences, defend your reading with one quotation from chapter 38, cited by chapter. Say plainly what evidence in the chapter supports your reading, and address at least one detail that could be read the other way.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who took a different position from yours. Point to one line in chapter 38 that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • This is a genuinely contested question among readers of this novel. There is no single correct answer; there is only a position you can defend from the text.
  • Consider both the marriage itself and the choice to close the book on St. John rather than on Jane and Rochester's household.
  • Ground your claim in the specific words of chapter 38, not in how you would feel about the ending in general.

discussions.title: Which Part of Jane's World Most Needs Explaining?
discussions.html:
Your Thornfield Chronicle explains one part of Jane's world to a reader who has never opened the book: the real position of a Victorian governess, the Gothic mode, inheritance and marriage law and money, or the shape of a coming-of-age story. A stranger to the novel would not automatically understand any of these on their own.

Post (by mid-week): Name the part of Jane's world you think most needs explaining to a reader who has never opened the book, and why. In four to six sentences, defend your choice with one cited detail from the novel (chapter) or from a credible source, and say plainly what a reader misses about the whole story if nobody explains it to them first.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who chose a different part of Jane's world. Ask them one honest question about how they plan to make their part clear to a total stranger, or point out one place a reader might still get lost.

Guidance

  • This is not "what is your Chronicle topic," though the two may match. Argue for why this piece of Jane's world is the one that most needs a guide.
  • Use the stranger test from the writing-for-a-stranger lesson: would the detail you cite make sense to someone who has never read the book?
  • A heading-shaped claim (a short noun phrase, not a full paragraph topic) is good practice for the section headings your Draft needs this week.

discussions.title: Why Open with a Fireman Who Loves the Fire?
discussions.html:
The novel's first sentence is "It was a pleasure to burn." (Fahrenheit 451, Part One). For several pages afterward, Bradbury makes destruction look beautiful, and the man doing it is the character we are asked to follow. Only later does a girl on a sidewalk start asking him questions.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: why does a novel against book-burning open by making book-burning a pleasure? In four to six sentences, argue your reading with one quotation copied from your own copy of Part One, cited as (Part One), and say what the opening pages gain that a sober, disapproving opening would lose. Try one deliberate fragment placed after a full sentence (see the lesson on the fragment and the simile).

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who read the opening differently. Point to one detail from the first pages that complicates their reading, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • Argue from the sentences, not from what you know the book is "about." Quote from your own copy and name the Part.
  • "It makes the reader complicit" is a real position; so is "it shows how good the society is at making harm feel like joy." Pick one and defend it, or argue a third.
  • One quotation is required. Copy it exactly; do not paraphrase it inside quotation marks.

discussions.title: The People, Not the Government
discussions.html:
Across his visit to Montag, Captain Beatty argues that the firemen did not invent this world. He says the public itself demanded faster entertainment, simpler books, and the removal of anything that might offend or unsettle anyone, and that burning books is really just where all those small, popular demands ended up.

Post (by mid-week): Take a position: is Beatty right about the world of the novel? Is he right about ours? In four to six sentences, argue your reading with one quotation copied from your own copy of Part One, cited as (Part One), and address both halves of the question, the novel's world and your own.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who answered at least one half of the question differently than you did. Point to a specific detail from their post and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • "He's right about the novel, and it's a warning about us too" is one position. "He's right about the novel, but the comparison to now is too easy" is another. Argue one, or a third of your own.
  • One quotation is required, copied exactly from your own copy and cited by Part.
  • If you compare Beatty's claim to the present day, be specific: name an actual habit, platform, or pattern, not just a general fear.

discussions.title: What a Book Leaves Behind
discussions.html:
Faber tells Montag, "It's not books you need, it's some of the things that once were in books." (Fahrenheit 451, Part Two). He means that a book is a container, not the thing itself, quality information, time to think about it, and the freedom to act on it.

Post (by mid-week): Name one specific thing you have learned from a book, any book, at any point in your life, that you do not think could have come from a screen the same way. In four to six sentences, explain what you learned and why the format (a book, read slowly, on your own terms) mattered to how you learned it. Include one quotation copied from your own copy of Part Two, cited as (Part Two), that supports or complicates your answer.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate whose example is different from yours. Ask whether their reasoning would also apply to a different format (an audiobook, a documentary, a long article) and why or why not.

Guidance

  • Be specific. "Books teach you empathy" is a start, not an answer. Name the book, the thing you learned, and the moment it landed.
  • Faber's claim is a challenge, not a compliment to books. Feel free to push back on it if your own experience disagrees.
  • One quotation from Part Two is required, copied exactly and cited correctly.

discussions.title: Socrates, Faber, and Beatty
discussions.html:
This week you met three well-read men. Socrates, on trial in Athens, tells the jury that "the unexamined life is not worth living" (Plato, Apology, excerpt B) and refuses every offer to buy his safety with silence. Faber, in this novel, once said something close to it: "It's not books you need, it's some of the things that once were in books" (Fahrenheit 451, Part Two), and then spent years saying nothing. Beatty has read enough to quote circles around anyone in the room, and burns books for a living anyway.

Post (by mid-week): All three are well-read men. What separates the one who keeps thinking in public from the one who burns? Take a position, in five to seven sentences, using one quotation from the Apology excerpts (given above, or another line from excerpts A1, A2, or B, quoted exactly) and one detail from your own copy of Part Two, cited (Part Two), describing something Faber or Beatty actually does. Do not summarize all three men; argue for what you think the real difference is.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who names a different difference than yours. Point to one specific detail in their reasoning you had not considered, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • "Socrates had courage and Beatty didn't" is a start, not an answer. Say what the courage was actually for: what Socrates refused to trade away that Beatty traded away without a fight.
  • Faber is not simply "the good one." He has his own failure in this scene; use it.
  • Quote the Apology exactly as it appears in the Socrates lesson; quote your own copy exactly as it appears in your edition.

discussions.title: Hero or Survivor?
discussions.html:
By the end of this week's reading, Montag has burned his own house, caused a man's death, run for his life, and crossed a river that leaves the city behind him. Montag's own explanation for the second of these is "Beatty wanted to die." (Fahrenheit 451, Part Three), an explanation the novel never fully confirms or denies.

Post (by mid-week): Is Montag a hero, or only a survivor? What has he become by the river? Take a position, in five to seven sentences, using one quotation from your own copy of Part Three, cited (Part Three), and address at least one cost of what he has done, not only what he has escaped.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who calls Montag something different than you did (hero, survivor, both, neither). Point to one detail in their reasoning you had not weighed, and ask one honest question about it.

Guidance

  • "Hero" and "survivor" are not opposites you must choose between cleanly; some of the strongest posts will argue Montag is both, and explain what that combination actually looks like.
  • Do not skip past Beatty's death to get to the river. A post that only discusses the escape without weighing what it cost is missing half the question.
  • Quote your own copy exactly, and cite the Part.

discussions.title: The Living Books Broadcast: Pitch Your Episode
discussions.html:
You are about to record the episode you have been building since Week 2. Before you do, pitch it here the way a producer would pitch it to a network deciding whether to air it, and name the argument a censor would make against you.

Post (by the end of Week 5), your pitch, in 5 to 7 sentences:

  1. What is the work or idea you preserve, in one sentence a listener could repeat back to a friend? Name the source (a text from this year, an independent-reading book, or a passage from your own copy of Fahrenheit 451) and why it must survive.
  2. What is your strongest opposing view, the censor's case against preserving this particular work or idea? State it as fairly and forcefully as you can, the way an honest opponent would make it, not as a strawman.
  3. Walk through your segment map in one or two sentences: your four segments (cold open, recitation, the case, the close) and their approximate timings.
  4. Name one source from your Show Bible you are proud of, and say why it holds up.

Reply (by the start of Week 6) to at least TWO classmates. For each reply, name one thing that would make their episode listenable to a stranger who has never heard of their chosen work, and ask one honest question, a place their segment map seems unbalanced, a claim that seems to need a stronger source, or a spot where their stated censor's case seems too easy to answer.

Guidance

  • A strong censor's case is not a joke version of the opposing view. If your censor's case is easy to knock down, it is not doing its job yet; strengthen it before you post, and strengthen it again before you record your actual episode in Week 7.
  • "Sounds cool" is not feedback. "Your segment map gives the cold open almost half your runtime, which may crowd out the case itself; have you timed a read-through?" is.
  • You are not co-producing anyone's episode. Every Living Books submission stays a solo piece; this discussion only trades feedback before recording begins.
  • This is one discussion spanning two weeks: it opens at the end of Week 5 and stays open through the start of Week 6, so check back for replies even after you post.

discussions.title: Memorizing to Save It
discussions.html:
Granger's book people cannot keep a single physical copy of anything. Instead, each person carries one whole text in memory, waiting for the moment paper and printing return. This year, once each quarter, you have done a small version of the same thing: memorized a passage and spoken it aloud, without a page in front of you.

Post (by mid-week): The book people memorize texts to save them from a society that has burned every copy. How does that practice answer the dystopia Bradbury builds across the novel, and how does it answer our own year of recitation? In four to six sentences, argue a real position, not a summary, and support it with one quotation cited either from your own copy of the novel (Part Three) or from the Ecclesiastes 3 / Revelation 22 text in the Ecclesiastes and Revelation lesson.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate whose answer names a different reason memorization matters. Point to a specific line from their post, and add one detail from the novel or the two Bible passages that either supports or complicates what they argued.

Guidance

  • Argue from what memorization actually does in the story (who it protects, what it makes possible when paper is not available) rather than restating the plot.
  • Bringing in your own recitation experience is expected and welcome: what has changed in you for carrying a passage by heart since your first one this year.
  • One quotation is required, cited by Part (for the novel) or by chapter and verse (for the King James text). Copy it exactly.

discussions.title: The First Voice on Air
discussions.html:
This week's lesson on the year in one question set six voices side by side: Hamlet, Publius, Emerson, Douglass, Jane, and Montag, each tested by a different pressure, each answering some version of what it means to govern oneself.

Post (by mid-week): Of the year's five voices before this novel, Hamlet, Publius, Emerson, Douglass, and Jane, which one would you put on air first, if you were building a broadcast like Montag's to preserve the year's best thinking about self-government? In four to six sentences, name the voice, say what you would have them say (in your own words, not a new invented quotation), and cite one quotation from that figure that you have already used or encountered this year, with its correct source.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to a classmate who chose a different voice. Say what your own choice's argument would add to theirs if the two aired back to back, and ask one honest question about their choice.

Guidance

  • Choosing a voice is a real argument: why does this one deserve to go first, ahead of the other four.
  • Use only quotations already taught this year (Hamlet, the Federalist, Emerson, Douglass, or Jane Eyre); do not invent a new one.
  • Cite correctly for that figure's genre: act and scene (Hamlet), paper number (Federalist), essay title (Emerson), chapter (Douglass's Narrative, or Jane Eyre).
